subject: physiology
title: The Chloride Shift, Carbonic Anhydrase, and Carbon Dioxide Transport

steps.tx: Metabolic carbon dioxide generated by cellular respiration is transported in systemic venous blood in three distinct fractions. While seven percent dissolves physically in aqueous plasma and twenty-three percent binds globin as carbaminohaemoglobin, roughly seventy percent of all transported carbon dioxide travels as **plasma bicarbonate ions**.
steps.say: Seventy percent of carbon dioxide travels as plasma bicarbonate, with the remainder dissolved or bound as carbaminohaemoglobin.

rows: Hydration by carbonic anhydrase in RBCs
Direct binding to N-terminal amino groups

steps.tx: The rapid conversion of carbon dioxide to bicarbonate within erythrocytes is catalyzed by the zinc metalloenzyme **carbonic anhydrase**, localized in immense quantities within red blood cell cytoplasm. Carbonic anhydrase accelerates the reversible hydration of carbon dioxide into carbonic acid by more than five orders of magnitude.
steps.say: Carbonic anhydrase inside red blood cells accelerates the reversible conversion of carbon dioxide into carbonic acid over ten-thousand-fold.

nodes.label: Cellular CO2 Enters Red Blood Cell via Simple Passive Diffusion
Carbonic Anhydrase (CA-II) Hydrates CO2 + H2O into Carbonic Acid (H2CO3)
Instantaneous Spontaneous Dissociation into H+ and Bicarbonate (HCO3-)
Protons Buffered by Deoxyhaemoglobin (Haldane Effect); HCO3- Accumulates

steps.tx: Once generated, carbonic acid dissociates instantaneously into hydrogen ions and bicarbonate ions. While hydrogen ions are buffered by deoxygenated haemoglobin through the Haldane effect, accumulating intracellular bicarbonate reaches high concentrations, driving its outward diffusion into venous plasma through the **anion exchanger 1** membrane transporter.
steps.say: Intracellular bicarbonate diffuses out into venous plasma across anion exchanger 1, also called band 3 protein.

nodes.label: CO2 Diffuses from Tissue into Erythrocyte Cytoplasm
Carbonic Anhydrase Converts CO2 + H2O into H2CO3 -> H+ + HCO3-
Deoxyhaemoglobin Buffers H+ Ions to Prevent Intracellular Acidosis
AE1 (Band 3): Electroneutral 1:1 Exchange of Outward HCO3- for Inward Cl-

steps.tx: To maintain electrical neutrality across the erythrocyte plasma membrane during outward bicarbonate egress, chloride ions enter the red blood cell in a strict one-to-one stoichiometry. This electroneutral exchange process is famously termed the **chloride shift**, or the Hamburger phenomenon, occurring within fractions of a second in tissue capillaries.
steps.say: The chloride shift maintains electroneutrality by moving chloride into the red cell as bicarbonate moves out into plasma.

left.title: Systemic Capillaries (Tissue Inflow)
points: CO2 enters RBC; converted to HCO3- and H+
Chloride (Cl-) shifts from plasma into erythrocyte
Intracellular osmoles increase, causing RBC swelling

right.title: Pulmonary Capillaries (Lung Outflow)
points: Bicarbonate enters RBC; chloride exits into plasma
CA converts HCO3- back to CO2 gas for exhalation
Intracellular osmoles drop; RBC shrinks slightly

steps.tx: Because chloride entry increases total intracellular osmoles within erythrocytes traversing systemic capillary beds, water enters osmotically down its concentration gradient. Consequently, venous red blood cells exhibit a slightly increased mean corpuscular volume, making the **venous haematocrit** approximately three percent higher than arterial haematocrit.
steps.say: Water enters red blood cells along with chloride, causing cell swelling and making venous haematocrit slightly higher than arterial haematocrit.

steps.tx: In pulmonary capillaries, the entire cascade reverses seamlessly. Inhaled oxygen binds haemoglobin, releasing buffered protons; the **reverse chloride shift** transfers chloride back out into plasma while bicarbonate re-enters the erythrocyte, where carbonic anhydrase dehydrates it back to carbon dioxide gas for alveolar exhalation.
steps.say: In the lungs, the reverse chloride shift moves chloride out and bicarbonate in, where carbonic anhydrase regenerates carbon dioxide for exhalation.

nodes.label: Pulmonary Capillaries: Oxyhaemoglobin Releases Buffered Protons (H+)
Reverse Chloride Shift: Plasma HCO3- Enters RBC; Cl- Exits into Plasma
Carbonic Anhydrase Hydrates Protons and HCO3- Back into H2O and CO2
CO2 Gas Diffuses Rapidly into Alveoli and Is Cleared via Expiration

steps.tx: Blocking one enzyme in the red cell and kidney explains most of this drug picture. **Acetazolamide** inhibits carbonic anhydrase, slowing carbon dioxide hydration so bicarbonate is lost in urine and a mild metabolic acidosis develops. That acidosis stimulates breathing, which is why the drug prevents mountain sickness, and reduced aqueous humour formation lowers eye pressure in glaucoma. Tingling fingers and a flat taste to fizzy drinks are its familiar minor costs.
steps.say: Acetazolamide blocks carbonic anhydrase, wasting bicarbonate and producing mild acidosis that stimulates breathing. It also lowers aqueous formation in glaucoma.

steps.tx: Pharmacological inhibition of carbonic anhydrase with **acetazolamide** slows the interconversion of carbon dioxide and bicarbonate throughout renal tubules and red blood cells. By inducing renal bicarbonate wasting and metabolic acidosis, acetazolamide stimulates central chemoreceptors, serving as a primary treatment for acute mountain sickness and sleep apnoea.
steps.say: Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase, causing mild metabolic acidosis that stimulates breathing to treat acute mountain sickness.

steps.tx: The non-bicarbonate portion of carbon dioxide transport relies on **carbaminohaemoglobin formation**, occurring without enzymatic catalysis. Carbon dioxide reacts directly with uncharged terminal alpha-amino groups on globin chains to generate carbamino compounds, which also release protons that contribute to the allosteric Bohr effect.
steps.say: Carbaminohaemoglobin forms spontaneously when carbon dioxide binds terminal amino groups, releasing protons that reinforce the Bohr effect.
